comments.content: The upper clamp of 10,000 attempts per window on a `sensitive: true` login endpoint means a misconfigured or leaked env var can effectively disable brute-force protection without any signal. Consider a much lower production cap (e.g. a few hundred) and/or gating the override to non-production environments (or at least logging a warning when an override is active in production), so weakening login rate limiting is an explicit, visible decision rather than a silent configuration change.

comments.content: Any authenticated non-admin user can claim ANY Person record by id, as long as it is VERIFIED and not yet linked to an account — I confirmed `claimPersonForUser` enforces only those two preconditions plus 'account not already linked'. There is no proof-of-identity binding (e.g., matching verified email, invitation token, or admin approval). This allows identity takeover: a user can enumerate/guess person ids and bind someone else's verified identity (with its history, affiliations, and contributions) to their own account. Consider requiring an identity-proof check for self-claims (e.g., verified email match between the account and the person record, or a claim token), or restricting self-claim to admin-initiated flows.
comments.thinking:
Confirmed: `requireRoleAccess` returns `AuthenticatedUser` (never NextResponse) and handles unauthorized via `redirect()` (which throws NEXT_REDIRECT). So in the merge routes:

```ts
const auth = await requireRoleAccess("en", ["ADMIN"]);
if (auth instanceof NextResponse) return auth;
```

The `instanceof NextResponse` check is dead code — it can never be true per the declared return type. This also means unauthorized admin API callers get an HTTP redirect to a dashboard HTML page instead of a 401/403 JSON response — a behavioral concern for an API route, though consistent with existing admin routes in the codebase (the modified GET routes use the same pattern). The dead-code `instanceof` check is worth flagging as maintainability/dead-code.

Also note: unauthenticated users get redirected to login page rather than 401 — pre-existing pattern across admin routes, so I won't push hard on it, but the dead instanceof check is clearly flag-worthy in both new merge routes.

Also issue 1: claim endpoint identity takeover. claimPersonForUser only requires VERIFIED + unlinked. Any authenticated user can claim any VERIFIED unlinked Person. The route has no additional proof-of-identity check. This is a genuine security concern — flag it on the claim route.

Issue 3: params.id (targetId) not validated as UUID in merge routes while sourceId is. The service resolves via resolvePersonId which does findUnique — a malformed id just returns null → 404 "Person not found." Not a crash (Prisma findUnique with malformed uuid string — for a String id field, Prisma won't throw). So minor inconsistency; low/medium. Worth a low comment.

comments.content: The cancel fast-path only triggers when the payload contains status CANCELLED and nothing else. `ActivityOccurrenceUpdateSchema` is `ActivityOccurrenceInputSchema.partial().strict()`, so `{ "status": "CANCELLED", "capacity": 5 }` (or with startsAt/locationJson) is a perfectly valid payload — it falls into `updateOccurrence`, which applies `status: "CANCELLED"` via a plain `update` with no `admittedCount` check. That bypasses the invariant enforced by `cancelOccurrence` (occupied occurrences cannot be cancelled) and can strand confirmed participants/participations. Either route every `status === "CANCELLED"` transition through `cancelOccurrence` (rejecting any additional fields explicitly), or add the same `admittedCount === 0` CAS guard to the status-transition path in `updateOccurrence`.
comments.thinking:
Issue 6: body parsing — `await req.json()` without catch; if body is invalid JSON it throws → 500. But that's pre-existing behavior (line 42 unchanged). `Object.keys(body ?? {})` — if body is a primitive like `5` or a string, Object.keys works (returns indices for strings, [] for numbers). If body is null, `?? {}` handles it. Object.keys on a non-null primitive won't throw. So no crash; but if body is e.g. `"title"`, destructuring later would yield undefined. The conflict check semantics are fine. Issue 6 is largely moot — the check is after parsing and slug check. One nuance: `req.json()` with empty/invalid body throws uncaught → 500, but that's pre-existing. Skip issue 6.

comments.content: The capacity-shrink CAS (`admittedCount: { lte: newCapacity }`) does not exclude a concurrent `claimOccurrenceSeat` that read the row before the shrink. Interleaving: claim reads capacity=3/admittedCount=1 → shrink to capacity=1 succeeds (admittedCount=1 ≤ 1) → claim's CAS on `admittedCount: 1` still matches and increments to 2 > capacity=1. This breaks the documented "never exceed capacity" guarantee. Make the check-and-increment atomic at the row level (e.g. a single raw statement `UPDATE ... SET "admittedCount" = "admittedCount" + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'SCHEDULED' AND (capacity IS NULL OR "admittedCount" < capacity)`), or include the previously read `capacity`/`admittedCount` in the shrink CAS condition and force claim to re-read after any capacity change.

Consider handling `existing.status === "APPROVED"` explicitly: return success idempotently when `existing.occurrenceId === occurrenceId`, and release-then-admit when it differs.

comments.content: Guardian (proxy) grants are authorized purely by caller-supplied fields: any authenticated user can grant consent on behalf of any other user by setting guardianUserId to their own id and attaching arbitrary self-asserted evidenceJson. I searched the codebase and found no independent guardian-relationship verification anywhere (no GuardianLink model or admin-verified relationship check) — evidenceJson is stored verbatim but never validated. Combined with listConsentsForSubject (which grants read access to anyone who has ever been a grantor for a subject), an attacker can forge consents for an arbitrary subject and then read that subject's full consent history. Since resolveConsent gates publication in publication-gateway.ts, forged consents also unblock publishing another user's data. Consider requiring a server-side verified guardian relationship (e.g., a GuardianLink record established through a verified flow) before accepting proxy grants, and treat evidenceJson as supporting metadata rather than the authorization mechanism.

comments.content: The new version number is computed via findMany + max inside the transaction, but the ConsentRecord model has no unique constraint on (subjectUserId, purpose, channel, objectType, objectId, version) — only a non-unique @@index([subjectUserId, purpose, status]). Consider adding a unique constraint at the schema level (note: nullable channel/object columns complicate this — a normalized scope key column or serializable transaction / advisory lock may be needed) so the database enforces the one-ACTIVE-per-scope invariant.

comments.content: The query is capped at take: 20 (latest ACTIVE versions for a subject+purpose) and channel/object matching happens in memory afterwards. Once a subject accumulates more than 20 ACTIVE consents for one purpose across different channels/objects (realistic with per-object consents, which are a designed feature), an older still-valid generic consent (channel/object = null) falls outside the window and resolution incorrectly returns null, blocking legitimate publications. Push the channel/object predicates into the database where clause (OR: null / exact match for each of channel, objectType, objectId) so the query returns only applicable consents instead of truncating before matching.

comments.content: This GET endpoint is fully unauthenticated ("公开读取") and returns every personId attached to an activity plus free-text `note` values, with no pagination. This route skips that check entirely, so person lists of programme-scoped activities are leaked publicly. At minimum, add the same `assertActivityScopeAccess` read check; ideally also require an authenticated session and consider omitting `note` from the public payload.

comments.content: Two non-idiomatic secret-generation patterns: (1) `generateChannelMachineKey` hashes `crypto.randomUUID()` (~122 bits entropy) instead of drawing bytes directly — use `crypto.randomBytes(24)` (or `getRandomValues`) and base64url-encode, which is the conventional idiom for API secrets. (2) `generateChannelClientKey` maps random bytes via `% alphabet.length` (36), which introduces modulo bias since 256 is not divisible by 36; low-risk for an identifier, but rejection sampling (`if (byte >= 252) continue`) or a 32-char alphabet (256 % 32 === 0) removes the bias cleanly.

comments.content: Account-link transfer violates the `Person.userId @unique` constraint on a real database. The code first sets `target.userId = source.userId` while the source row still holds that same userId, so Postgres rejects the first UPDATE with a unique-violation and the whole merge transaction rolls back with a generic 500. Any merge where the source person is linked to an account (and the target is not) will therefore always fail in production — even though the in-memory test double passes because it never enforces uniqueness. Clear the source first, then assign the target (or do it in a single statement).

comments.content: Version numbering for asset-only evidence versions is race-prone: this read-then-create computes max+1, but `@@unique([recordId, version])` in the Prisma schema never fires when `recordId` is NULL (NULLs are distinct in Postgres), so two concurrent creates on the same asset can both persist the same version number. Two concurrent runs of the admin process route both observe `status === "QUEUED"` and both send the email (duplicate user-facing mail); the `updateMany` guard only decides who wins the status write afterwards. Similarly, `attemptNumber = previousAttempts.length + 1` is computed outside the transaction, so concurrent attempts can record duplicate attempt numbers. Consider a CAS claim (e.g. `updateMany` QUEUED→SENDING) before any external send, and deriving the attempt number inside the claim transaction.

comments.content: This catch-and-requery idempotency path cannot work inside the caller's interactive transaction on PostgreSQL. All callers (`admin/certificates/[id]/revoke`, `restore`, `publication-gateway`, `source-activity-mapping`) pass a `tx` handle from `prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => ...)`; once the `create` fails with P2002, Postgres puts the transaction in aborted state and Prisma does not wrap statements in savepoints, so the `findUnique` below throws "current transaction is aborted" — turning an idempotent replay into a 500 that rolls back the whole business write. The mock-based tests can't see this because the fake tx stays usable after errors. Restructure: use `upsert` keyed on `idempotencyKey`, or pre-check with `findUnique` before `create` (still handling the race by letting P2002 propagate and re-reading after rollback outside the transaction).

comments.content: The lease CAS does not actually isolate claimed rows. After `updateMany` claims a subset of `due`, this re-fetch selects by `id IN (due) AND status = PROCESSING` — which matches rows claimed by *any* concurrent worker, not just the ones this invocation won (`claimed.count` is never used to identify which ids were claimed). With two concurrent processors, worker B claims 0 rows but still sees all of worker A's freshly-claimed PROCESSING rows here and delivers them a second time, defeating the lease and duplicating external callbacks. Claim per-row (single-row `updateMany` CAS and skip on count 0) or tag the lease with an owner token and filter the re-fetch by it.

comments.content: Two state-machine gaps here: (a) the update unconditionally sets `status: SUCCEEDED`/`deliveredAt`, so reconciling a DEAD or still-PENDING dispatch silently resurrects it as delivered; (b) the idempotency check reads `stored.receipt`/`stored.reconciledRevision`, but the success path in `processOutboundDispatches` stores receipts in a different shape (`{ httpStatus, body, receivedAt, revision }`), so after a real delivery `sameReceipt` never matches and a reconcile overwrites the original delivery receipt — destroying the evidence this module exists to keep. Normalize one receipt shape for both paths and only allow reconcile transitions from SUCCEEDED (or explicitly handle DEAD/PENDING).

comments.content: `callbackUrl` is validated as https-off-localhost at registration (`validateCallbackUrl` in channel-client-auth.ts), which is good — but `fetch` follows redirects by default, so a validated https callback can 302 the worker to `http://169.254.169.254/...` or other internal addresses, keeping an SSRF primitive alive via redirect. Use `redirect: "manual"` (treat 3xx as a non-retryable or dead-letter response) or re-validate every redirect target before following.

Files: 1. notification-delivery.ts: - HTML injection (high) — lines around 122-125. - No CAS claim / duplicate send + attempt number race (medium) — processDueNotifications findMany + deliverNotification flow. - SMS latent trap (low) — the EMAIL/SMS comment block. 2. reliable-dispatch.ts: - P2002 catch in tx (high) — enqueueOutboundDispatch catch block. - Lease CAS re-fetch (high) — rows findMany. - reconcile shape mismatch + unconditional SUCCEEDED (medium). - idempotencyKey cast (low) + maybe canonicalize undefined note. - SSRF redirect follow (low). 3. Migration outbox: low reentrancy. 4. Migration privacy: low reentrancy (CREATE INDEX without IF NOT EXISTS). 5. Tests: loose `!=` (low). Maybe also that the source-regex test is brittle? Skip. Let me write the comments. Keep concise. Comment 1 (high, security, notification-delivery.ts): existing_code: ``` const subject = notification.titleEn ?? notification.title; const text = [notification.titleEn ?? notification.title, notification.actionUrl ? `Open: ${notification.actionUrl}` : ""] .filter(Boolean) .join("\n\n"); try { const { sendTransactionalMail } = await import("./mailer"); await sendTransactionalMail({ to: recipient.email, subject, html: `

${text.replace(/\n/g, "
")}

`, text }); ``` Content: `text` (title/actionUrl) is interpolated into the HTML body with no escaping; mailer.ts passes `html` straight to Resend. Module docs say programme owns wording, so title can carry external/party-controlled text → HTML injection in trusted-sender email. Suggest escaping. Comment 2 (high, bug, reliable-dispatch.ts) — P2002: existing_code: ``` } catch (error) { if (typeof error === "object" && error !== null && "code" in error && (error as { code?: string }).code === "P2002") { const existing = await tx.outboundDispatch.findUnique({ ``` Content: callers (revoke/restore, publication-gateway, source-activity-mapping) pass interactive-transaction handles; on Postgres a failed statement aborts the transaction, so the findUnique in the catch throws "current transaction is aborted", rolling back the business write on idempotent replay. Suggest upsert or catch outside the transaction / re-query after rollback. Comment 3 (high, bug, reliable-dispatch.ts) — lease CAS: existing_code: ``` const rows = await prisma.outboundDispatch.findMany({ where: { id: { in: due.map((row) => row.id) }, status: DISPATCH_PROCESSING }, include: { channelClient: { select: { callbackUrl: true, key: true } } }, }); ``` Content: re-fetch matches any PROCESSING row in the candidate set, including rows claimed by a concurrent worker (claimed.count is never tied to specific ids). Two concurrent processors both deliver the same dispatch → duplicate external callbacks. Suggest per-row CAS claim loop or filtering by the lease owner token. Comment 4 (medium, bug, notification-delivery.ts) — no claim before send: existing_code: ``` const due = await prisma.notification.findMany({ where: { status: "QUEUED", deadLetteredAt: null, OR: [{ nextRetryAt: null }, { nextRetryAt: { lte: now } }], }, ``` And in deliverNotification the email is sent before the guarded updateMany; concurrent runs both pass status === QUEUED and both send. Also attemptNumber from previousAttempts.length outside tx can duplicate. Suggest CAS claim (updateMany status QUEUED→SENDING) before sending. Comment 5 (medium, bug, reliable-dispatch.ts) — reconcile: existing_code: ``` const stored = row.receiptJson as { receipt?: unknown; reconciledRevision?: number } | null; const sameReceipt = stored?.receipt !== undefined && hashDispatchPayload(stored.receipt) === hashDispatchPayload(input.receipt) && stored.reconciledRevision === input.revision; if (row.status === DISPATCH_SUCCEEDED && sameReceipt) { return { ok: true, id: row.id, applied: false }; } await prisma.outboundDispatch.update({ where: { id: row.id }, data: { receiptJson: { receipt: input.receipt, reconciledAt: new Date().toISOString(), reconciledRevision: input.revision } as Prisma.InputJsonValue, status: DISPATCH_SUCCEEDED, deliveredAt: new Date(), }, }); ``` Content: (a) success path stores `{httpStatus, body, receivedAt, revision}` — no `receipt` key — so sameReceipt never matches after real delivery; reconcile overwrites original receipt evidence. (b) unconditional SUCCEEDED resurrects DEAD/PENDING rows. Suggest normalizing receipt shape and guarding status transitions. Comment 6 (low, security, reliable-dispatch.ts) — SSRF redirect: existing_code: deliverDispatchOverHttp fetch. callbackUrl validated https at registration (channel-client-auth.validateCallbackUrl), but fetch follows redirects by default — a validated https endpoint can 302 to internal addresses. Suggest `redirect: "manual"` or revalidating redirect targets. Comment 7 (low, maintainability, reliable-dispatch.ts) — idempotencyKey cast: existing_code: ``` "X-Dispatch-Idempotency-Key": (row as { idempotencyKey?: string }).idempotencyKey ?? row.id, ``` Content: DispatchRow omits idempotencyKey, forcing an ad-hoc cast; add the field to DispatchRow. Also canonicalize maps undefined→"null" making {a:undefined} and {a:null} hash equal — document or handle. Comment 8 (low, migration privacy) — CREATE INDEX without IF NOT EXISTS. Comment 9 (low, migration outbox) — ADD COLUMN/CREATE INDEX without IF NOT EXISTS inconsistent with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS. Comment 10 (low, test) — loose != in matches helpers. Rule says == / != prohibited. Both test files. I'll comment on notification-privacy.test.mjs matches helper; mention the same pattern in reliable-dispatch.test.mjs. Comment 11 (low, notification-delivery) — SMS channel falls through to email send. No SMS producers today (search confirmed), but comment claims EMAIL/SMS share transport; an opted-in SMS notification would be emailed to the user's email address. Suggest explicit channel guard. Should I also comment on the test asserting error message "unexpected import"? That's brittle but tests-only; skip. Also the test file notification-privacy: `row[key] != null` appears multiple times — comment once. Order comments by file. Let me write them.
